entries.3695d6534c88214d57ab19ee0f5784c86b38f03f: <div sID="gen8756" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Neh.3" sID="Neh.3"/> <div eID="gen8756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8757" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> Saying and doing are often two things: many are ready to say, "Let us rise up and build," who sit still and do nothing, like that fair-spoken son who said,"I go, Sir, but went not." The undertakers here were none of those. As soon as they had resolved to build the wall about Jerusalem they lost no time, but set about it presently, as we find in this chapter. Let it never be said that we left that good work to be done to-morrow which we might as well have done to-day. This chapter gives an account of two things:—I. The names of the builders, which are recorded here to their honour, for they were such as herein discovered a great zeal for God and their country, both a pious and a public spirit, a great degree both of industry and courage; and what they did was fit to be thus largely registered, both for their praise and for the encouragement of others to follow their example. II. The order of the building; they took it before them, and ended where they began. They repaired, 1. From the sheep-gate to the fish-gate, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.1-Neh.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. 2. Thence to the old-gate, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.3-Neh.1.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. 3. Thence to the valley-gate, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.6-Neh.1.12">ver. 6-12</reference>. 4. Thence to the dung-gate, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.13-Neh.1.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. 5. Thence to the gate of the fountain, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.15">ver. 15</reference>. 6. Thence to the water-gate, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.16-Neh.1.26">ver. 16-26</reference>. 7. Thence by the horse-gate to the sheep-gate again, where they began (<reference osisRef="Neh.1.27-Neh.1.32">ver. 27-32</reference>), and so they brought their work quite round the city.
entries.eab71c753450a55655e3b436f91449b9df9d6550: <div eID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8757" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Rebuilding of the Wall. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 445.)</title> <div sID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests, and they builded the sheep gate; they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it; even unto the tower of Meah they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And next unto him builded the men of Jericho. And next to them builded Zaccur the son of Imri. <hi type="super">3</hi> But the fish gate did the sons of Hassenaah build, who <hi type="italic">also</hi> laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof. <hi type="super">4</hi> And next unto them repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Koz. And next unto them repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabeel. And next unto them repaired Zadok the son of Baana. <hi type="super">5</hi> And next unto them the Tekoites repaired; but their nobles put not their necks to the work of their Lord. <hi type="super">6</hi> Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah; they laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks thereof, and the bars thereof. <hi type="super">7</hi> And next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon, and of Mizpah, unto the throne of the governor on this side the river. <hi type="super">8</hi> Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of <hi type="italic">one of</hi> the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall. <hi type="super">9</hi> And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> And next unto them repaired Jedaiah the son of Harumaph, even over against his house. And next unto him repaired Hattush the son of Hashabniah. <hi type="super">11</hi> Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashub the son of Pahathmoab, repaired the other piece, and the tower of the furnaces. <hi type="super">12</hi> And next unto him repaired Shallum the son of Halohesh, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, he and his daughters. <hi type="super">13</hi> The valley gate repaired Hanun, and the inhabitants of Zanoah; they built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate. <hi type="super">14</hi> But the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Beth-haccerem; he built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof. <hi type="super">15</hi> But the gate of the fountain repaired Shallun the son of Colhozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David. <hi type="super">16</hi> After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Beth-zur, unto <hi type="italic">the place</hi> over against the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty. <hi type="super">17</hi> After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani. Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part. <hi type="super">18</hi> After him repaired their brethren, Bavai the son of Henadad, the ruler of the half part of Keilah. <hi type="super">19</hi> And next to him repaired Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah, another piece over against the going up to the armoury at the turning <hi type="italic">of the wall.</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> After him Baruch the son of Zabbai earnestly repaired the other piece, from the turning <hi type="italic">of the wall</hi> unto the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. <hi type="super">21</hi> After him repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz another piece, from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of the house of Eliashib. <hi type="super">22</hi> And after him repaired the priests, the men of the plain. <hi type="super">23</hi> After him repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house. After him repaired Azariah the son of Maaseiah the son of Ananiah by his house. <hi type="super">24</hi> After him repaired Binnui the son of Henadad another piece, from the house of Azariah unto the turning <hi type="italic">of the wall,</hi> even unto the corner. <hi type="super">25</hi> Palal the son of Uzai, over against the turning <hi type="italic">of the wall,</hi> and the tower which lieth out from the king's high house, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> by the court of the prison. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh. <hi type="super">26</hi> Moreover the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto <hi type="italic">the place</hi> over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out. <hi type="super">27</hi> After them the Tekoites repaired another piece, over against the great tower that lieth out, even unto the wall of Ophel. <hi type="super">28</hi> From above the horse gate repaired the priests, every one over against his house. <hi type="super">29</hi> After them repaired Zadok the son of Immer over against his house. After him repaired also Shemaiah the son of Shechaniah, the keeper of the east gate. <hi type="super">30</hi> After him repaired Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, another piece. After him repaired Meshullam the son of Berechiah over against his chamber. <hi type="super">31</hi> After him repaired Malchiah the goldsmith's son unto the place of the Nethinims, and of the merchants, over against the gate Miphkad, and to the going up of the corner. <hi type="super">32</hi> And between the going up of the corner unto the sheep gate repaired the goldsmiths and the merchants. <div eID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8760" type="x-p"/> The best way to know how to divide this chapter is to observe how the work was divided among the undertakers, that every one might know what he had to do, and mind it accordingly with a holy emulation, and desire to excel, yet without any contention, animosity, or separate interest. No strife appears among them but which should do most for the public good. Several things are observable in the account here given of the building of the wall about Jerusalem:— <div eID="gen8760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> I. That Eliashib the high priest, with his brethren the priests, led the van in this troop of builders, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Ministers should be foremost in every good work; for their office obliges them to teach and quicken by their example, as well as by their doctrine. If there be labour in it, who so fit as they to work? if danger, who so fit as they to venture? The dignity of the high priest was very great, and obliged him to signalize himself in this service. The priests repaired the <hi type="italic">sheep-gate,</hi> so called because through it were brought the sheep that were to be sacrificed in the temple; and therefore the priests undertook the repair of it because <hi type="italic">the offerings of the Lord made by fire were</hi> their inheritance. And of this gate only it is said that <hi type="italic">they sanctified it</hi> with the word and prayer, and perhaps with sacrifices perhaps, 1. Because it led to the temple; or, 2. Because with this the building of the wall began, and it is probable (though they were at work in all parts of the wall at the same time) that this was first finished, and therefore at this gate they solemnly committed their city and the walls of it to the divine protection; or, 3. Because the priests were the builders of it; and it becomes ministers above others, being themselves in a peculiar manner sanctified to God, to sanctify to him all their performances, and to do even their common actions <hi type="italic">after a godly sort.</hi> <div eID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8762" type="x-p"/> II. That the undertakers were very many, who each took his share, some more and some less, in this work, according as their ability was. Note, What is to be done for the public good every one should assist in, and further, to the utmost of his place and power. United force will conquer that which no individual dares venture on. Many hands will make light work. <div eID="gen8762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8763" type="x-p"/> III. That many were active in this work who were not themselves inhabitants of Jerusalem, and therefore consulted purely the public welfare and not any private interest or advantage of their own. Here are the men of Jericho with the first (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.2">v. 2</reference>), the men of Gibeon and Mizpah (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.7">v. 7</reference>), and Zanoah, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.13">v. 13</reference>. Every Israelite should lend a hand towards the building up of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen8763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> IV. That several rulers, both of Jerusalem and of other cities, were active in this work, thinking themselves bound in honour to do the utmost that their wealth and power enabled them to do for the furtherance of this good work. But it is observable that they are called rulers of <hi type="italic">part,</hi> or the <hi type="italic">half part,</hi> of their respective cities. One was <hi type="italic">ruler of the half part of Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.12">v. 12</reference>), another of part of Beth-haccerem (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.14">v. 14</reference>), another of part of Mizpah (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">v. 15</reference>), another of <hi type="italic">the half part of Beth-zur</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.16">v. 16</reference>), one was ruler of <hi type="italic">one half part,</hi> and another of <hi type="italic">the other half part, of Keilah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.3.17-Neh.3.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. Perhaps the Persian government would not entrust any one with a strong city, but appointed two to be a watch upon each other. Rome had two consuls. <div eID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8765" type="x-p"/> V. Here is a just reproach fastened upon the nobles of Tekoa, that they <hi type="italic">put not their necks to the work of their Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">v. 5</reference>), that is, they would not come under the yoke of an obligation to this service; as if the dignity and liberty of their peerage were their discharge from serving God and doing good, which are indeed the highest honour and the truest freedom. Let not nobles think any thing below them by which they may advance the interests of their country; for what else is their nobility good for but that it puts them in a higher and larger sphere of usefulness than that in which inferior persons move? <div eID="gen8765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> VI. Two persons joined in repairing <hi type="italic">the old gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">v. 6</reference>), and so were co-founders, and shared the honour of it between them. The good work which we cannot compass ourselves we must be thankful to those that will go partners with us in. Some think that this is called the <hi type="italic">old gate</hi> because it belonged to the ancient Salem, which was said to be first built by Melchizedek. <div eID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8767" type="x-p"/> VII. Several good honest tradesmen, as well as priests and rulers, were active in this work—<hi type="italic">goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.32">32</reference>. They did not think their callings excused them, nor plead that they could not leave their shops to attend the public business, knowing that what they lost would certainly be made up to them by the blessing of God upon their callings. <div eID="gen8767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8768" type="x-p"/> VIII. Some ladies are spoken of as helping forward this work—<hi type="italic">Shallum and his daughters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.12">v. 12</reference>), who, though not capable of personal service, yet having their portions in their own hands, or being rich widows, contributed money for buying materials and paying workmen. St. Paul speaks of some good women that <hi type="italic">laboured with him in the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.3">Phil. iv. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen8768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8769" type="x-p"/> IX. Of some it is said that they repaired <hi type="italic">over against their houses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.10">v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.28">28,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.29">29</reference>), and of one (who, it is likely, was only a lodger) that he repaired <hi type="italic">over against his chamber,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.3.30">v. 30</reference>. When a general good work is to be done each should apply himself to that part of it that falls nearest to him and is within his reach. If every one will sweep before his own door, the street will be clean; if every one will mend one, we shall be all mended. If he that has but a chamber will repair before that, he does his part. <div eID="gen8769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> X. Of one it is said that he <hi type="italic">earnestly</hi> repaired that which fell to his share (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.20">v. 20</reference>)—he did it with an inflamed zeal; not that others were cold or indifferent, but he was the most vigorous of any of them and consequently made himself remarkable. It is good to be thus <hi type="italic">zealously affected in a good thing</hi> and it is probable that this good man's zeal provoked very many to take the more pains and make the more haste. <div eID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8771" type="x-p"/> XI. Of one of these builders it is observed that he was <hi type="italic">the sixth son</hi> of his father, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.30">v. 30</reference>. His five elder brethren, it seems, laid not their hand to this work, but he did. In doing that which is good we need not stay to see our elders go before us; if they decline it, it does not therefore follow that we must. Thus the younger brother, if he be the better man, and does God and his generation better service, is indeed the better gentleman; those are most honourable that are most useful. <div eID="gen8771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> XII. Some of those that had <hi type="italic">first done helped their fellows,</hi> and undertook another share where they saw there was most need. Meremoth repaired, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4">v. 4</reference> and again, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">v. 21</reference>. And the Tekoites, besides the piece they repaired (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">v. 5</reference>), undertook another piece (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">v. 27</reference>), which is the more remarkable because their nobles set them a bad example by withdrawing from the service, which, instead of serving them for an excuse to sit still, perhaps made them the more forward to do double work, that by their zeal they might either shame or atone for the covetousness and carelessness of their nobles. <div eID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8773" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is no mention of any particular share that Nehemiah himself had in this work. A name-sake of his is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.16">v. 16</reference>. But did he do nothing? Yes, though he undertook not any particular piece of the wall, yet he did more than any of them, for he had the oversight of them all; half of his servants worked where there was most need, and the other half stood sentinel, as we find afterwards (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.16">ch. iv. 16</reference>), while he himself in his own person walked the rounds, directed and encouraged the builders, set his hand to the work where he saw occasion, and kept a watchful eye upon the motions of the enemy, as we shall find in the next chapter. The pilot needs not haul at a rope: it is enough for him to steer.  <chapter eID="Neh.3"/> <div eID="gen8773" type="x-p"/>

entries.60c7d87172a27415db443226487f1653fcfca882: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4310"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.3.1-Neh.3.32">Ne 3:1-32</reference>. The Names and Order of Them That Builded the Wall of Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen6252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4310"/><hi type="bold">1. Then Eliashib the high priest--</hi>the grandson of Jeshua, and the first high priest after the return from Babylon.<div eID="gen6252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rose up with his brethren the priests--</hi>that is, set an example by commencing the work, their labors being confined to the sacred localities.<div eID="gen6253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they builded the sheep gate--</hi>close to the temple. Its name arose either from the sheep market, or from the pool of Bethesda, which was there (<reference osisRef="John.5.2">Joh 5:2</reference>). There the sheep were washed and then taken to the temple for sacrifice.<div eID="gen6254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they sanctified it, and set up the doors--</hi>Being the common entrance into the temple, and the first part of the building repaired, it is probable that some religious ceremonies were observed in gratitude for its completion. "It was the first-fruits, and therefore, in the sanctification of it, the whole lump and building was sanctified" [Poole].<div eID="gen6255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the tower of Meah--</hi>This word is improperly considered, in our version, as the name of a tower; it is the Hebrew word for "a hundred," so that the meaning is: they not only rebuilt the sheep gate, but also a hundred cubits of the wall, which extended as far as the tower of Hananeel. <div eID="gen6256" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a4f12c92e4a0c82a6c4210312c52ca618f9b240: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4311"/><div sID="gen6257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4311"/><hi type="bold">2. next unto him builded the men of Jericho, &c.--</hi>The wall was divided into portions, one of which was assigned respectively to each of the great families which had returned from the captivity. This distribution, by which the building was carried on in all parts simultaneously with great energy, was eminently favorable to despatch. "The villages where the restorers resided being mostly mentioned, it will be seen that this circumstance affords a general indication of the part of the wall upon which they labored, such places being on that side of the city nearest their place of abode; the only apparent exception being, perhaps, where they repaired more than their piece. Having completed their first undertaking (if they worked any more), there being no more work to be done on the side next their residence, or having arrived after the repairs on that part of the city nearest them under operation were completed, they would go wherever their services would be required" [Barclay, City of the Great King]. <div eID="gen6257" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a4969dbf81362ccb828206a55bdebde49b8f94c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4312"/><div sID="gen6258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4312"/><hi type="bold">8. they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall--</hi>or, "double wall," extending from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits in length, formerly broken down by Joash, king of Israel [2Ch 25:23], but afterwards rebuilt by Uzziah [2Ch 26:9], who made it so strong that the Chaldeans, finding it difficult to demolish, had left it standing. <div eID="gen6258" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d2091ab1a367e73074fb238d6d18976cd743456: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4313"/><div sID="gen6259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4313"/><hi type="bold">12. Shallum ... he and his daughters--</hi>who were either heiresses or rich widows. They undertook to defray the expenses of a part of the wall next them. <div eID="gen6259" type="x-p"/>
entries.d86e326a182896e0f8699897ca154e597d31b3d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4314"/><div sID="gen6260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4314"/><hi type="bold">13. the inhabitants of Zanoah--</hi>There were two towns so called in the territory of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.34">Jos 15:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.56">56</reference>). <div eID="gen6260" type="x-p"/>
entries.940f46841aaa183b295c8ff34d3874704a7f7c9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4315"/><div sID="gen6261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4315"/><hi type="bold">14. Beth-haccerem--</hi>a city of Judah, supposed to be now occupied by Bethulia, on a hill of the same name, which is sometimes called also the mountain of the Franks, between Jerusalem and Tekoa. <div eID="gen6261" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f6a762a38afde5829322d68d2dcf5ba18088847: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4316"/><div sID="gen6262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4316"/><hi type="bold">16. the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty--</hi>that is, along the precipitous cliffs of Zion [Barclay]. <div eID="gen6262" type="x-p"/>
entries.a96f29d33b461b76983deb416812a3a934d8e462: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4317"/><div sID="gen6263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4317"/><hi type="bold">19. at the turning of the wall--</hi>that is, the wall across the Tyropoeon, being a continuation of the first wall, connecting Mount Zion with the temple wall [Barclay]. <div eID="gen6263" type="x-p"/>
entries.9919c72703f791a5c3f8a23df18adcc351042ebf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4318"/><div sID="gen6264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4318"/><hi type="bold">25. the tower which lieth out from the king's high house--</hi>that is, watchtower by the royal palace [Barclay]. <div eID="gen6264" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b08774aa8643895912110a7808fcfae477e63d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4319"/><div sID="gen6265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4319"/><hi type="bold">26. the Nethinims--</hi>Not only the priests and the Levites, but the common persons that belonged to the house of God, contributed to the work. The names of those who repaired the walls of Jerusalem are commemorated because it was a work of piety and patriotism to repair the holy city. It was an instance of religion and courage to defend the true worshippers of God, that they might serve Him in quietness and safety, and, in the midst of so many enemies, go on with this work, piously confiding in the power of God to support them [Bishop Patrick]. <chapter eID="Neh.3"/>

entries.87258ce83db4542da9a41d1e8cb1330057f86c6b: <div eID="gen14983" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14984" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14984" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14986" type="x-p"/> The names of those who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem; and the part assigned to each person, vv. 1-32. <div eID="gen14986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14988" type="x-p"/> Eliashib the high priest - It was right that the priests should be first in this holy work; and perhaps the sheep gate which is mentioned here is that by which the offerings or sacrifices were brought into the temple. <div eID="gen14988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> They sanctified it - As they began with the sacred offering as soon as they got an altar built, it was proper that the gate by which these sacrifices entered should be consecrated for this purpose, i. e., set apart, so that it should be for this use only.
entries.fb7ef884044e538ad0f0d0bc9962a352a4028bba: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14990" type="x-p"/> The fish gate - We really know scarcely any thing about these gates - what they were, why called by these names, or in what part of the wall situated. All plans of Jerusalem, its temple, walls, and gates, are mere works of conjecture; and yet how learnedly have some men written on all these subjects!
entries.5c26c8e811241419c7945431f37747f3874758ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14991" type="x-p"/> The throne of the governor - His house, and the place where he dispensed justice and judgment. Previously to the days of Nehemiah, Jerusalem was governed by a deputy from the Persian king; (see <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh 5:15</reference>); but after this time they were governed by governors and judges chosen from among themselves.
entries.020e5b46a2d7fde8ea8e06e42a77e5955856ab5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen14991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14992" type="x-p"/> Goldsmiths - From the remotest period of the history of the Jews they had artists in all elegant and ornamental trades; and it is also evident that goldsmiths, apothecaries, and merchants were formed into companies in the time of Nehemiah. <div eID="gen14992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14993" type="x-p"/> Apothecaries - Rather such as dealt in drugs, aromatics, spices, etc., for embalming, or for furnishing the temple with the incense consumed there.
entries.71f817795515f0ed992c3c0fd2c4fbc76ab94986: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14994" type="x-p"/> Ruler of the half part of Jerusalem - Probably the city was divided into two parts; one for Judah, and the other for Benjamin, each having its proper governor. Rephaiah mentioned here was one of these governors, and Shallum, mentioned <reference osisRef="Neh.3.12">Neh 3:12</reference>, was the other. There were other rulers or governors of particular country or village districts.
entries.58f9d6859baf9a8cf2df23675f1608bee5379b87: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen14994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14995" type="x-p"/> Repaired the other piece - That which was left by Jedaiah after he had repaired the wall opposite to his own house. Probably some of the principal people were obliged to repair those parts of the wall opposite to their own dwellings. Perhaps this was the case generally.
entries.00f20b26abf037276c647c6412412b3877dc8073: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen14995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14996" type="x-p"/> The son of Halohesh - Or, the son of the Enchanter: conjectured to be thus named from having the art to charm serpents. <div eID="gen14996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14997" type="x-p"/> The ruler of the half part - See on <reference osisRef="Neh.3.9">Neh 3:9</reference> (note).
entries.7180ae973caf577012facefbfdfa928b333a2869: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen14997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14998" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Zanoah - This was a town in the tribe of Judah. <reference osisRef="Jos.15.34">Jos 15:34</reference>.
entries.9dba07058ec9861272ee13ef770d98df8a65721d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen14998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14999" type="x-p"/> Beth-haccerem - A village or town in the tribe of Benjamin. See <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jer 6:1</reference>.
entries.bdbe25713ca57f6afcabcd4a80d53e57db0f9089: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen14999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15000" type="x-p"/> The pool of Siloah - This is probably the same as that mentioned by the evangelists. <div eID="gen15000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15001" type="x-p"/> The stairs that go down from the city of David - Jerusalem being built on very uneven ground, and some hills being taken within the walls; there was a necessity that there should be in different places steps by which they could ascend and descend: probably similar to what we see in the city of Bristol.
entries.20703c348b475f38ebd68f928d080307ad860373: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen15001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15002" type="x-p"/> The pool that was made - Calmet supposes that this was the reservoir made by Hezekiah, when besieged by Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.4">2Chr 32:4</reference>. <div eID="gen15002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15003" type="x-p"/> The house of the mighty - Probably a place where a band of soldiers was kept, or the city guard.
entries.89c50bfd6d9a52fe8e4b9afcb3d876a7115b467d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen15003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15004" type="x-p"/> The going up to the armoury - This was either a tower that defended the angle where the two walls met; or the city arsenal, where shields, spears, etc., were kept to arm the people in time of danger.
entries.845e75d84320bb38046737f7512e724617555473: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen15004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15005" type="x-p"/> Earnestly repaired - He distinguished himself by his zeal and activity.
entries.d1374940fefc7e1567b83b61b6023c674764315e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen15005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15006" type="x-p"/> The priests, the men of the plain - Some of the officers of the temple, particularly the singers, dwelt in the plain country round about Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Neh.12.28">Neh 12:28</reference>; and it is likely that several of the priests dwelt in the same place.
entries.5247ede475e77894f9135c588067279a32a3a28f: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen15006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15007" type="x-p"/> The horse gate - The place through which the horses passed in order to be watered; It was near the temple. Some rabbins suppose that in order to go to the temple, a person might go on horseback to the place here referred to, but then was obliged to alight, as a horse could pass no farther. Horses were never very plentiful in Jerusalem.
entries.9fcdeb94c877216965da6b6743cd3436bac9f340: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen15007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15008" type="x-p"/> The goldsmiths and the merchants - The word הצרפים hatstsorephim may signify smiths, or persons who worked in metals of any kind; but it is generally understood to mean those who worked in gold. I have already observed, that the mention of merchants and goldsmiths shows that these persons were formed into bodies corporate in those ancient times. But these terms are differently rendered in the versions. The Vulgate is the same as ours, which probably our translators copied: aurifices et negociatores. The Syriac is, goldsmiths and druggists. The Arabic, smelters of metal and porters. The Septuagint, in some copies, particularly in the Roman edition, and in the Complutensian, Antwerp, and Paris Polyglots, have οἱ χαλκεις και οἱ μεταβολι, smiths and merchants; but in other copies, particularly the London Polyglot, for μεταβολοι we find ῥωποπωλαι, seller of shields. And here the learned reader will find a double mistake in the London Polyglot, ῥοποπωλαι for ῥωποπωλαι, and in the Latin version scruta for scuta, neither of which conveys any sense.  <chapter eID="Neh.3"/> <div eID="gen15008" type="x-p"/>

entries.0c461628af740cf682e5922c35aeb6d6ecf3cdef: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Neh 3:1</reference> <div eID="gen6508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6509" type="x-p"/> The narrative of the building is connected with what precedes by ויּקם, which alludes to the carrying out of the resolve, נקוּם, Neh 2:18. The enumeration begins with Eliashib the high priest and his brethren, i.e., the ordinary priests. These built the sheep-gate, rightly sought by modern topographers in the eastern wall north of Haram, the site of the ancient temple, i.e., in the position or neighbourhood of the present St. Stephen’s gate, through which the Bedouins to this day drive sheep into the town for sale (Tobler, <hi type="italic">Topogr</hi>. i. p. 149). “Although,” as Bertheau remarks, “we are not generally justified, after the lapse of so many centuries, during which great changes have been made in the positions of the gates and walls, and in face of the fact that the present walls and gates were not erected till the years 1536, 1537, and 1539, in determining the direction and extent of the walls between the several gates, and the locality of the gates in this description, by the direction and extent of the wall and the locality of the gates in modern Jerusalem (Tobl. <hi type="italic">Topogr. Dritte Wanderung</hi>, p. 265), yet in the present instance valid arguments exist in favour of this view. The very neighbourhood of the temple and the nature of the soil bear witness that from ancient times a gate was placed here which took its name from the circumstance that sheep were driven in by it, whether for sale in the market or for sacrificial purposes.”<note placement="foot">In the neighbourhood of this gate was the pool of Bethesda (Joh 5:2), i.e., either the present <hi type="italic">Birket Israel</hi> or <hi type="italic">Birket es Serain</hi>, south of St. Stephen’s gate (Tobler, <hi type="italic">Denkblätter</hi>, p. 53f., and <hi type="italic">Dritte Wanderung</hi>, p. 221), or the Struthion pool mentioned by Josephus, <hi type="italic">bell. Jud</hi>. v. 11. 4, κολυμβήθρα τοῦ στρουθίου; Krafft, <hi type="italic">Topographie von Jerusalem</hi>, p. 127f.</note> <div eID="gen6509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6510" type="x-p"/> They sanctified it and set up its doors: and to the tower Hammeah they sanctified it unto the tower Hananeel. קדּשׁ, to sanctify, to dedicate (comp. 1Ki 8:64), can here only mean that the priests dedicated that portion of building on which they were engaged, as soon as they had finished it, for the purpose of sanctifying the whole work by this preliminary consecration; the solemn dedication of the whole wall not taking place till afterwards, and being related Neh 12:27. The setting up of the doors in the gates did not, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.6.1">Neh 6:1</reference>, take place till after all the breaches in the wall had been repaired, i.e., till the building of the wall was completed. It is, however, mentioned here, and in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.3">Neh 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Neh 3:6</reference>, etc., contemporaneously with the wall-building; because the builders of the several gates, undertaking also the construction and setting up of the doors, the intention is to give a summary of the work executed by the respective building parties. המּאה ועד־מגּדּל is still dependent on יבנוּ, that is to say, this verb must be mentally repeated before the words: they built to the tower Hammeah, they sanctified it (the suffix in קדּשׁוּהוּ can only relate to מגּדּל). יבנוּ must also be repeated before חננאל מגּדּל עד: and they built further, unto the tower Hananeel. The tower המּאה (the hundred) is only mentioned here and <reference osisRef="Neh.12.39">Neh 12:39</reference>, but the tower Hananeel is likewise spoken of <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38">Jer 31:38</reference> and Zec 14:10. From these passages it appears that the two towers were so situated, that any one going from west to east along the north wall of the city, and thence southward, would first come to the tower Hananeel, and afterwards to the tower Hammeah, and that both were between the fish-gate and the sheep-gate. From the passages in Jeremiah and Zechariah especially, it is evident that the tower Hananeel stood at the north-east corner of the wall. Hence the statement in this verse, that the portion of wall built by the priests extended to the north-east corner of the wall; and the tower Hammeah must be sought between the sheep-gate and the north-east corner of the wall. Whence the names of these towers were derived is unknown.
entries.d564b8881417ab49440eb57a2f1f6f80296f314a: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.2">Neh 3:2</reference> <div eID="gen6510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6511" type="x-p"/> Next to him built the men of Jericho (comp. Ezr 2:24); and next to them built Zaccur the son of Imri. The suffix of the first ידו על, though in the singular number, refers to Eliashib and the priests (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.1">Neh 3:1</reference>), and that of the second to the men of Jericho, while in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4">Neh 3:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.9">Neh 3:9</reference>, on the contrary, a singular noun is followed by ידם על; both ידו על and ידם על expressing merely the notion beside, next to, and builders of the respective portions being at one time regarded as in a plural, at another in a singular sense (as a company). The portion built by the men of Jericho and Zaccur the son of Imri, the head of a family, not mentioned elsewhere, let between the tower Hananeel and the fish-gate in the north wall. When individuals are, like Zaccur, mentioned in the following description, e.g., <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4">Neh 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Neh 3:6</reference>, as builders or repairers of portions of wall, they are heads of houses who engaged in the work of building at the head of the fathers of families and individuals who were dependent on them.
entries.ec84574fc02fdb3778ad04e25b841007da947f72: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.3">Neh 3:3</reference> <div eID="gen6511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6512" type="x-p"/> The fish-gate did the sons of Senaah build (see rem. on Ezr 2:35); they laid its beams, and set up its doors, bolts, and bars. The fish-gate probably received its name from the fish-market in its neighbourhood, to which the Syrians brought sea-fish (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.13">Neh 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.16">Neh 3:16</reference>); it is also mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.12.39">Neh 12:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">2Ch 33:14</reference>, and Zep 1:10. It was not situated, as Thenius has represented it in his plan of Jerusalem, close to the corner tower of Hananeel, but somewhat to the west of it in the north wall; two lengths of wall being, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.2">Neh 3:2</reference>, built between this tower and the gate in question. With respect to קרוּהוּ, see rem. on Neh 2:8. Besides the doors for the gate, מנעוּיו and בּריחיו are mentioned, as also <reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Neh 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.13">Neh 3:13</reference>-15. Both words denote bars for closing doors. בּרחים are, to judge from the use of this word in the description of the tabernacle (Exo 26:26. and elsewhere), longer bars, therefore cross-bars, used on the inner side of the door; and מנעוּלים the brackets into which they were inserted.
entries.cd0b9ff596cb5a11c5197da1620dfc07448c207d: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4-Neh.3.5">Neh 3:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen6512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6513" type="x-p"/> Next to these, Meremoth the son of Urijah, the son of Hakkoz, Meshullam the son of Berechiah, Zadok the son of Baana, and the Tekoites, repaired in the above order, each a portion of wall. החזיק, to strengthen, means here to repair the gaps and holes in the wall; comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.3.9">Neh 3:9</reference>, Neh 3:27. Meremoth ben Urijah repaired, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference>, another portion besides. Meshullam ben Berechiah was, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.6.18">Neh 6:18</reference>, a person of consideration in Jerusalem. The men of Tekoa, who do not occur among those who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2), also repaired a second portion. “But their nobles brought not their neck to the service of their Lord.” The expression “to bring the neck to service” is, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.27.11">Jer 27:11</reference>, to be understood as meaning: to bring the neck under the yoke of any one, i.e., to subject oneself to the service of another. צוּרם stands for צוּארם. It is questionable whether אדניהם is to be taken as the plural of excellence, and understood of God, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">Deu 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.3">Psa 135:3</reference>; Mal 1:6; or of earthly lords or rulers, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.40.1">Gen 40:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">2Sa 10:3</reference>; 1Ki 12:27. The former view seems to us decidedly correct, for it cannot be discerned how the suffix should (according to Bertheau’s opinion) prevent our thinking of the service of God, if the repairing of the wall of Jerusalem may be regarded as a service required by God and rendered to Him. Besides, the fact that אדנים is only used of kings, and is inapplicable whether to the authorities in Jerusalem or to Nehemiah, speaks against referring it to secular rulers or authorities.
entries.5e89305194d11e12a5036f64a00d4d7def8aaa12: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Neh 3:6</reference> <div eID="gen6513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6514" type="x-p"/> From the gate of the old wall to the valley gate. - <reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Neh 3:6</reference> הישׁנה שׁער does not mean the old gate, for הישׁנה is genitive. Schultz (<hi type="italic">Jerus</hi>. p. 90), Thenius, and Bertheau supply העיר, gate of the old town, and explain the name from the fact that Bezetha, the new town, already existed as a suburb or village in front of the gate, which was named after the contrast. To this Arnold rightly objects (in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Realencycl</hi>. xviii. p. 628) that it is by no means proved that there was at that time any contrast between the old and new towns, and as well as Hupfeld (<hi type="italic">die topograph. Streitfragen über Jerus.</hi>, in the <hi type="italic">morgenl. Zeitschrift</hi>, xv. p. 231) supplies חומה: gate of the old wall. He does not, however, derive this designation from the remark (vv. <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">Neh 3:8</reference>), “They fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall,” as though this old wall received its name from having been left undestroyed by the Chaldeans, which is irreconcilable with the fact (4-8) that both the gate of the old wall and the portions of wall adjoining it on each side were now built, but understands the term “old wall” as used in contrast to the “broad wall,” which had indeed been rebuilt after the destruction by Joash (2Ki 14:13). This view we esteem to be correct. The individuals specified as the builders of this gate are not further known. That two <hi type="italic">principes</hi> were employed in the rebuilding of this gate is explained by Ramb. as arising <hi type="italic">vel quod penitus disturbata a Chaldaeis, vel quod magnis sumtibus reparanda fuit, quos unus princeps ferre non potuit</hi>.
entries.1fca3f7c7c8d058f4587fec8c2fe4a1abd6ab842: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.7">Neh 3:7</reference> <div eID="gen6514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6515" type="x-p"/> Next unto them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite, and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon and of Mizpah. If Melatiah is to be regarded as the superintendent of the men of Gibeon, Jadon the Meronothite must be equally esteemed that of the men of Mizpah. Meronoth, mentioned only here and <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.30">1Ch 27:30</reference>, must have been some small place near Mizpah. Mizpah (המּצפּה, the watch-tower) is probably the modern <hi type="italic">Nebi Samwil</hi>, two leagues to the north-east of Jerusalem; see rem. on Jos 19:26. The meaning of the words next following, וגו פּחת לכּסּא, is questionable. Bertheau, together with Osiander, Cler., de Wette, and others, understands them as more precisely defining the men before named, as men of Gibeon and Mizpah, of the throne or belonging to the throne of the Pechah of Eber hannahar. This addition brings to light the fact that Jews who were not under the jurisdiction of Nehemiah, nevertheless took part in the restoration of the wall. It also distinguishes these men of Mizpah from those mentioned <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, who were certainly not under the Pechah of Eber hannahar. Finally, the boundary of the little territory of the returned Jewish community must have been at about Mizpah and Gibeon; and a statement that certain inhabitants of this district were not under the Pechah of Jerusalem, but under the Pechah of the province west of Euphrates, would agree with the position of Gibeon and Mizpah. None, however, of these reasons are of much force. For if, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">Neh 3:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, the Tekoites repaired two different lengths of wall, without this fact implying any distinction between these two parties of Tekoite builders, the same may be the case with the men of Gibeon and Mizpah. Besides, neither in this verse nor in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference> are the men of Mizpah in general spoken of, so as to make a distinction necessary; for in this verse two chiefs, Melatiah and Jadon, are designated as men of Gibeon and Mizpah, and in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference> two rulers of the district of Mizpah are specified by name. Hence the view that part of the inhabitants of Mizpah were under the jurisdiction of the Pechah of the province west of Euphrates, and part under that of the Pechah of Jerusalem, is devoid of probability. Finally, there is no adequate analogy for the metonomy set up in support of this view, viz., that כּסּא, a seat, a throne, stands for jurisdiction. The words in question can have only a local signification. כּסּא may indeed by metonomy be used for the official residence, but not for the official or judicial district, or jurisdiction of the Pechah. לכּסּא does not state the point to which, but the direction or locality in which, these persons repaired the wall: “towards the seat of the Pechah,” i.e., at the place where the court or tribunal of the governor placed over the province on this side Euphrates was held when he came to Jerusalem to administer justice, or to perform any other official duties required of him. This being so, it appears from this verse that this court was within the northern wall, and undoubtedly near a gate.
entries.513ad8ab064e36a2a9d85b7658a3f3dc795c38af: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">Neh 3:8</reference> <div eID="gen6515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6516" type="x-p"/> Next to him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah of the goldsmiths, and next to him repaired Hananiah, a son of the apothecaries. צורפים is in explanatory apposition to the name Uzziel, and the plural is used to denote that his fellow-artisans worked with him under his direction. Hananiah is called בּן־הרקּחים, son of the apothecaries, i.e., belonging to the guild of apothecaries. The obscure words, וגו ויּעזבוּ, “and they left Jerusalem unto the broad wall,” have been variously interpreted. From <reference osisRef="Neh.12.38">Neh 12:38</reference>, where the broad wall is also mentioned, it appears that a length of wall between the tower of the furnaces and the gate of Ephraim was thus named, and not merely a place in the wall distinguished for its breadth, either because it stood out or formed a corner, as Bertheau supposes; for the reason adduced for this opinion, viz., that it is not said that the procession went along the broad wall, depends upon a mistaken interpretation of the passage cited. The expression “the broad wall” denotes a further length of wall; and as this lay, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.12.38">Neh 12:38</reference>, west of the gate of Ephraim, the conjecture forces itself upon us, that the broad wall was that 400 cubits of the wall of Jerusalem, broken down by the Israelite king Joash, from the gate of Ephraim unto the corner gate (2Ki 14:13), and afterwards rebuilt by Uzziel of a greater breadth, and consequently of increased strength (Joseph. <hi type="italic">Antiq</hi>. ix. 10. 3). Now the gate of Ephraim not being mentioned among the rebuilt gates, and this gate nevertheless existing (according to <reference osisRef="Neh.8.16">Neh 8:16</reference>) in the days of Nehemiah, the reason of this omission must be the circumstance that it was left standing when the wall of Jerusalem was destroyed. The remark, then, in this verse seems to say the same concerning the broad wall, whether we understand it to mean: the builders left Jerusalem untouched as far as the broad wall, because this place as well as the adjoining gate of Ephraim needed no restoration; or: the Chaldeans had here left Jerusalem, i.e., either the town or town-wall, standing. So Hupfeld in his above-cited work, p. 231; Arnold; and even older expositors.<note placement="foot">Bertheau’s interpretation of this statement, viz., that at the rebuilding and re-fortification of the town after the captivity, the part of the town extending to the broad wall was left, i.e., was not rebuilt, but delayed for the present, answers neither to the verbal sense of the passage nor to the particular mentioned <reference osisRef="Neh.12.38">Neh 12:38</reference>, that at the dedication of the wall the second company of them that gave thanks went upon the wall from beyond the tower of the furnaces even unto the broad wall, and over from beyond the gate of Ephraim, etc. Haneberg (in Reusch’s theol. Literaturbl. 1869, No. 12) supports this view, but understands by “the broad wall” the wall which had a broad circuit, i.e., the wall previous to the captivity, and hence infers that the Jerusalem now rebuilt was not equal in extent to the old city. But if a portion of the former city had here been left outside the new wall, the gate of Ephraim would have been displaced, and must have been rebuilt elsewhere in a position to the south of the old gate. Still less can the attempt of the elder Buxtorf (Lexic. talm. rabb. s. v. עזב), now revived by Ewald (Gesch. iv. p. 174), to force upon the word עזב the meaning restaurare, or fortify, be justified.</note>
entries.ddcb8288c063ca7b5794279560dff8f30e096e33: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.9-Neh.3.10">Neh 3:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen6516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6517" type="x-p"/> Further lengths of wall were built by Rephaiah ben Hur, the ruler of the half district of Jerusalem, i.e., of the district of country belonging to Jerusalem (comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference>, where Mizpah and the district of Mizpah are distinguished); by Jedaiah ben Harumaph, בּיתו ונגד, and indeed before (opposite) his house, i.e., the portion of wall which lay opposite his own dwelling; and by Hattush the son of Hashabniah. Whether Hattush is to be identified with the priest of this name (<reference osisRef="Neh.10.5">Neh 10:5</reference>), or with the similarly named descendant of David (Ezr 8:2), or with neither, cannot be determined.
entries.20ab6698f79ad25a2a374676559ca1cfb4b07652: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.11">Neh 3:11</reference> <div eID="gen6517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6518" type="x-p"/> A second section of wall was repaired by Malchijah the son of Harim, and Hashshub ben Pahath-Moab, two families who came up with Zerubbabel, Ezr 2:6 and Ezr 2:32. Bertheau understands שׁנית מדּה of a second section of wall added to a first already repaired by the same builders. So, too, he says, did Meremoth ben Urijah build one portion, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4">Neh 3:4</reference>, and a second, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference>; comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">Neh 3:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">Neh 3:8</reference> and Neh 3:30. This first portion, however, which this mention of a second presupposes, not being named, he infers that our present text has not preserved its original completeness, and thinks it probable, from <reference osisRef="Neh.12.38">Neh 12:38</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.12.39">Neh 12:39</reference>, that certain statements, in this description, relating to the gate of Ephraim and its neighbourhood, which once stood before <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">Neh 3:8</reference>, have been omitted. This inference is unfounded. The non-mention of the gate of Ephraim is to be ascribed, as we have already remarked on <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">Neh 3:8</reference>, to other reasons than the incompleteness of the text; and the assertion that שׁנית מדּה assumes that a former portion was repaired by the same builders, receives no support from a comparison of <reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">Neh 3:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.8">Neh 3:8</reference> with Neh 3:30. Hananiah the son of Shelemiah, and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, who, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.30">Neh 3:30</reference>, built שׁני מדּה, are not identical with Hananiah the son of the apothecaries, Neh 3:8. The same remark applies to Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>), and Shallum the ruler of the district of Mizpah (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference>). Only in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.5">Neh 3:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4">Neh 3:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference>, are the names of the builders the same. Moreover, besides <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, שׁנית מדּה occurs five times more (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.11">Neh 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.20">Neh 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.24">Neh 3:24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.30">Neh 3:30</reference>) with respect to builders not previously (nor subsequently) mentioned in this list. Hence, in five different places, the names of the building parties, and the notices of the portions of wall built by them respectively, must have been lost, - a circumstance <hi type="italic">à priori</hi> incredible. When, however, we consider the verses, in which שׁנית מדּה occurs, more closely, the second length is, in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.20">Neh 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.24">Neh 3:24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, more nearly defined by a statement of locality: thus, in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, we have a second piece over against the ascent to the arsenal at the angle; in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.20">Neh 3:20</reference>, a second piece from the angle to the door of the house of Eliashib; in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference>, a second piece from the door of the house of Eliashib to ... ; in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.24">Neh 3:24</reference>, a second piece from the house of Azariah to ... , who, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.23">Neh 3:23</reference>, built near his own house; in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference>, a second piece over against the great projecting tower ... , as far as which, according to <reference osisRef="Neh.3.26">Neh 3:26</reference>, the Nethinim dwelt in Ophel. From all this, it is evident that שׁנית מדּה in these verses, always denotes a second portion of that length of wall previously spoken of, or a portion next to that of which the building was previously mentioned. And so must שׁנית מדּה be understood in the present <reference osisRef="Neh.3.11">Neh 3:11</reference>, where it is used because Malchiah and Hashshub repaired or built the tower of the furnaces, besides the portion of wall. שׁנית מדּה may be rendered, “another or a further piece.” the word שׁנית is chosen, because that previously mentioned is regarded as a first. The tower of the furnaces lay, according to this verse and <reference osisRef="Neh.12.38">Neh 12:38</reference>, where alone it is again mentioned, between the broad wall and the valley-gate. Now, since there was between the gate of Ephraim and the corner-gate a portion of wall four hundred cubits long (see 2Ki 14:13), which, as has been above remarked, went by the name of the broad wall, it is plain that the tower of the furnaces must be sought for in the neighbourhood of the corner-gate, or perhaps even identified with it. This is the simplest way of accounting for the omission of any notice in the present description of this gate, which is mentioned not merely before (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.9">2Ch 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.38">Jer 31:38</reference>; and 2Ki 14:13), but also after, the captivity (Zec 14:10). It is probable that the tower of the furnaces served as a defence for the corner-gate at the north-western corner of the town, where now lie, upon an earlier building of large stones with morticed edges, probably a fragment of the old Jewish wall, the ruins of the ancient <hi type="italic">Kal'at el Dshalud</hi> (tower of Goliath), which might, at the time of the Crusades, have formed the corner bastion of the city: comp. Rob. <hi type="italic">Palestine</hi>, ii. p. 114; <hi type="italic">Biblical Researches</hi>, p. 252; and Tobler, <hi type="italic">Topogr</hi>. i. p. 67f.
entries.85293b71eb50f2e9263f8c885910dd044ed62860: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.12">Neh 3:12</reference> <div eID="gen6518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6519" type="x-p"/> Next repaired Shallum, ruler of the other (comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.3.9">Neh 3:9</reference>) half district of Jerusalem, he and his daughters. הוּא can only refer to Shallum, not to הוּא, which would make the daughters signify the daughters of the district, of the villages and places in the district.
entries.29d3ea98f1ec635c56d3499b08aa61cd3247e220: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.13-Neh.3.14">Neh 3:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen6519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6520" type="x-p"/> From the valley-gate to the dung-gate. The <hi type="italic">valley-gate</hi> lay in the west, in the neighbourhood of the present Jaffa gate (see rem. on <reference osisRef="Neh.2.13">Neh 2:13</reference>), ”where,” as Tobler, <hi type="italic">Topogr</hi>. i. p. 163, expresses it, “we may conclude there must almost always have been, on the ridge near the present citadel, the site in the time of Titus of the water-gate also (Joseph. <hi type="italic">bell. Jud</hi>. v. 7. 3), an entrance provided with gates.” Hanun and the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Zanoah</hi> are here connected, probably because Hanun was the chief or ruler of the inhabitants of this place. <hi type="italic">Zanoah</hi>, now <hi type="italic">Zanna</hi>, is in the <hi type="italic">Wady Ismail</hi>, west of Jerusalem; see rem. on Jos 15:34. They built and set up its doors, etc.; comp. Neh 3:6. The further statement, “and a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung-gate,” still depends on החזיק, the principal verb of the verse. It is incomprehensible how Bertheau can say that this statement does not refer to the repairing of the wall, but only declares that the distance from the valley-gate to the dung-gate amounted to one thousand cubits. For the remark, that a section of such a length is, in comparison with the other sections, far too extensive, naturally proves nothing more than that the wall in this part had suffered less damage, and therefore needed less repair. The number one thousand cubits is certainly stated in round numbers. The length from the present Jaffa gate to the supposed site of the dung-gate, on the south-western edge of Zion, is above two thousand five hundred feet. The dung-gate may, however, have been placed at a greater distance from the road leading to <hi type="italic">Baher</hi>. השׁפות is only another form for האשׁפּות (without א prosthetic). Malchiah ben Rechab, perhaps a Rechabite, built and fortified the dung-gate; for though the Rechabites were forbidden to build themselves houses (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.7">Jer 35:7</reference>), they might, without transgressing this paternal injunction, take part in building the fortifications of Jerusalem (Berth.). This conjecture is, however, devoid of probability, for a Rechabite would hardly be a prince or ruler of the district of Beth-haccerem. The name Rechab occurs as early as the days of David, 2Sa 4:5. בּית־הכּרם, i.e., the garden or vineyard-house, where, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jer 6:1</reference>, the children of Benjamin were wont to set up a banner, and to blow the trumpet in Tekoa, is placed by Jerome (Comm. Jer 6) upon a hill between Jerusalem and Tekoa; on which account Pococke (<hi type="italic">Reise</hi>, ii. p. 63) thinks Beth-Cherem must be sought for on the eminence now known as the Frank mountain, the Dshebel Fureidis, upon which was the Herodium of Josephus. This opinion is embraced with some hesitation by Robinson (<hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 397), and unreservedly by Wilson (<hi type="italic">The Holy City</hi>, i. p. 396) and v. de Velde, because “when we consider that this hill is the highest point in the whole district, and is by reason of its isolated position and conical shape very conspicuous, we shall find that no other locality better corresponds with the passage cited.
entries.f4b6138e8ae17a6c1302d4df79e3a7ad8df00153: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> <div eID="gen6520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6521" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">fountain-gate</hi> and a portion of wall adjoining it was repaired by Shallum the son of Col-hozeh, the ruler of the district of Mizpah. כּל־חזה occurs again, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.5">Neh 11:5</reference>, apparently as the name of another individual. To יבננּוּ is added יטללנּוּ, he covered it, from טלל, to shade, to cover, answering to the קרוּהוּ of <reference osisRef="Neh.3.3">Neh 3:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.6">Neh 3:6</reference>, probably to cover with a layer of beams. The position of the fountain-gate is apparent from the description of the adjoining length of wall which Shallum also repaired. This was “the wall of the pool of Shelach (Siloah) by the king’s garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David.” The word שׁלח recalls שׁלּוח; the pool of Shelach can be none other than the pool which received its water through the שׁלח, i.e., <hi type="italic">mission</hi> (<hi type="italic">aquae</hi>). By the researches of Robinson (<hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 148f.) and Tobler (<hi type="italic">Die Siloahquelle u. der Oelberg</hi>, p. 6f.), it has been shown that the pool of Siloah receives its water from a subterranean conduit 1750 feet long, cut through the rock from the Fountain of the Virgin, <hi type="italic">Ain Sitti Miriam</hi>, on the eastern slope of Ophel. Near to the pool of Siloah, on the eastern declivity of Zion, just where the Tyropoean valley opens into the vale of Kidron, is found an old and larger pool (<hi type="italic">Birket el Hamra</hi>), now covered with grass and trees, and choked with earth, called by Tobler the lower pool of Siloah, to distinguish it from the one still existing, which, because it lies north-west of the former, he calls the upper pool of Siloah. One of these pools of Siloah, probably the lower and larger, is certainly the king’s pool mentioned <reference osisRef="Neh.2.14">Neh 2:14</reference>, in the neighbourhood of which lay, towards the east and south-east, the king’s garden. The wall of the pool of Shelach need not have reached quite up to the pool, but may have gone along the edge of the south-eastern slope of Zion, at some distance therefrom. In considering the next particular following, ”unto the stairs that go down from the city of David,” we must turn our thoughts towards a locality somewhat to the north of this pool, the description now proceeding from the south-eastern corner of the wall northward. These stairs are not yet pointed out with certainty, unless perhaps some remains of them are preserved in the “length of rocky escarpment,” which Robinson (<hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 102, and <hi type="italic">Biblical Researches</hi>, p. 247) remarked on the narrow ridge of the eastern slope of the hill of Zion, north of Siloam, at a distance of 960 feet from the present wall of the city, ”apparently the foundations of a wall or of some similar piece of building.”<note placement="foot">Bertheau’s view, that these stairs were situated where Mount Zion, upon which stood the city of David, descends abruptly towards the east, and therefore on the precipice running from south to north, which still rises ninety-one feet above the ground northwards of the now so-called Bab el Mogharibeh or dung-gate, opposite the southern part of the west wall of the temple area, is decidedly incorrect. For this place is two thousand feet, i.e., more than one thousand cubits, distant from the pool of Siloah, while our text places them immediately after the length of wall by this pool. The transposition of these “steps” to a position within the present wall of the city is, in Bertheau’s case, connected with the erroneous notion that the fountain-gate (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.2.14">Neh 2:14</reference>) stood on the site of the present dung-gate (<hi type="italic">Bab el Mogharibeh</hi>), for which no other reason appears than the assumption that the southern wall of the city of David, before the captivity, went over Zion, in the same direction as the southern wall of modern Jerusalem, only perhaps in a rather more southerly direction, - an assumption shown to be erroneous, even by the circumstance that in this case the sepulchres of David, Solomon, and the kings of Judah would have stood outside the city wall, on the southern part of Zion; while, according to the Scripture narrative, David, Solomon, and the kings of Judah were buried in the city of David (1Ki 2:10; 1Ki 11:42; 1Ki 14:31; 1Ki 15:8, and elsewhere). But apart from this consideration, this hypothesis is shattered by the statements of this fifteenth verse, which Bertheau cannot explain so inconsistently with the other statements concerning the building of the wall, as to make them say that any one coming from the west and going round by the south of the city towards the east, would first arrive at the fountain-gate, and then at the portion of wall in question; but is obliged to explain, so that the chief work, the building of the fountain-gate, is mentioned first; then the slighter work, the reparation of a length of wall <hi type="italic">as supplementary;</hi> and this makes the localities enumerated in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.13">Neh 3:13</reference> succeed each other in the following order, in a direction from the west by south and east towards the north: “Valley-gate - one thousand cubits of wall as far as the dung-gate; dung-gate - the wall of the conduit towards the king’s garden, as far as the stairs which lead from the city of David - fountain-gate.” No adequate reason for this transposition of the text is afforded by the circumstance that no portion of wall is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.14">Neh 3:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference>) as being repaired between the dung-gate and the valley-gate. For how do we know that this portion on the southern side of Zion was broken down and needing repair? Might not the length between these two gates have been left standing when the city was burnt by the Chaldeans?</note>
entries.d0925d5545b6ebd560f38c7418b80dff5be9f882: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.16-Neh.3.17">Neh 3:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen6521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6522" type="x-p"/> The wall from the steps leading from the city of David to the angle opposite the armoury. From <reference osisRef="Neh.3.16">Neh 3:16</reference> onwards we find for the most part אחריו, after him, instead of ידו על, which only occurs again in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.17">Neh 3:17</reference> and Neh 3:19. Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of half the district of Beth-zur (see rem. on <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.7">2Ch 11:7</reference>), repaired the wall as far as “opposite the sepulchres of David, and unto the pool that was made, and to the house of the heroes.” The sepulchres of David are the sepulchres of the house of David in the city of David (comp. <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.33">2Ch 32:33</reference>). “Opposite the sepulchres of David” is the length of wall on the eastern side of Zion, where was probably, as Thenius endeavours to show in the <hi type="italic">Zeitschr</hi>. of the <hi type="italic">deutsch morgenl. Gesellsch</hi>. xxi. p. 495f., an entrance to the burying-place of the house of David, which was within the city. The “pool that was made” must be sought at no great distance, in the Tyropoean valley, but has not yet been discovered. The view of Krafft (<hi type="italic">Topographie von Jerusalem</hi>, p. 152), that it was the reservoir artificially constructed by Hezekiah, between the two walls for the water of the old pool (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>), rests upon incorrect combinations. “The house of the heroes” is also unknown. In <reference osisRef="Neh.3.17">Neh 3:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.18">Neh 3:18</reference>, the lengths of wall repaired by the three building parties there mentioned are not stated. “The Levites, Rehum the son of Bani,” stands for: the Levites under Rehum the son of Bani. There was a Rehum among those who returned with Zerubbabel, <reference osisRef="Neh.12.3">Neh 12:3</reference>; Ezr 2:2; and a Bani occurs among the Levites in Neh 9:5. After him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of half the district of Keilah, for his district. Keilah, situate, according to <reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1">1Sa 23:1</reference>, in the hill region, is probably the village of Kila, discovered by Tobler (vol. iii. p. 151), eastward of Beit Dshibrin. By the addition לפלכּו, for his district, i.e., that half of the whole district which was under his rule, “it is expressly stated that the two halves of the district of Keilah worked apart one from the other” (Bertheau). The other half is mentioned in the verse next following.
entries.0e48c9ad2b3cab4b0490b6d2c6f6e39ffc1370be: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.18">Neh 3:18</reference> “Their brethren” are the inhabitants of the second half, who were under the rule of Bavai the son of Henadad.
entries.e71f1c4d3866f8ade6566c30fdb8cbad7debd597: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference> <div eID="gen6522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6523" type="x-p"/> Next to these repaired Ezer the son of Jeshua, the ruler of Mizpah, another piece (on שׁנית מדּה, see rem. on <reference osisRef="Neh.3.11">Neh 3:11</reference>) opposite the ascent to the armoury of the angle. הנּשׁק or הנּשׁק (in most editions) is probably an abbreviation of בּית־הנּשׁק, arsenal, armoury; and המּקצוע is, notwithstanding the article in הנּשׁק, genitive; for to combine it as an accusative with עלותּ, and read, “the going up of the armoury upon the angle,” gives no suitable meaning. The locality itself cannot indeed be more precisely stated. The armoury was probably situate on the east side of Zion, at a place where the wall of the city formed an angle; or it occupied an angle within the city itself, no other buildings adjoining it on the south. The opinion of Bertheau, that the armoury stood where the tower described by Tobler (<hi type="italic">Dritte Wand</hi>. p. 228) stands, viz., about midway between the modern Zion gate and the dung-gate, and of which he says that “its lower strata of stones are undoubtedly of a remoter date than the rebuilding of the wall in the sixteenth century,” coincides with the assumption already refuted, that the old wall of the city of David passed, like the southern wall of modern Jerusalem, over Mount Zion.
entries.38f657dec2221140185e5a286bb53acec5ab7732: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.20-Neh.3.21">Neh 3:20-21</reference> <div eID="gen6523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6524" type="x-p"/> The wall from the angle to the place of the court of the prison by the king’s upper house. - <reference osisRef="Neh.3.20">Neh 3:20</reference> After him Baruch the son of Zabbai emulously repaired a second length of wall, from the angle to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. Bertheau objects to the reading החרה, and conjectures that it should be ההרה, “up the hill.” But the reason he adduces, viz., that often as the word החזיק occurs in this description, a further definition is nowhere else added to it, speaks as much against, as for his proposed alteration; definitions of locality never, throughout the entire narrative, preceding החזיק, but uniformly standing after it, as also in the present verse. Certainly החרה cannot here mean either to be angry, or to be incensed, but may without difficulty be taken, in the sense of the Tiphal תּחרה, to emulate, to contend (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer 12:5</reference>), and the perfect adverbially subordinated to the following verb (comp. Gesen. <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §142, 3, a). The Keri offers זכּי instead of זבּי, probably from Ezr 2:9, but on insufficient grounds, the name זבּי occurring also Ezr 10:28. Of the position of the house of Eliashib the high priest, we know nothing further than what appears from these Ezr 10:20 and Ezr 10:21, viz., that it stood at the northern part of the eastern side of Zion (not at the south-western angle of the temple area, as Bertheau supposes), and extended some considerable distance from south to north, the second length of wall built by Meremoth reaching from the door at its southern end to the תּכלית, termination, at its northern end. On Meremoth, see rem. on Neh 3:4.
entries.0952962253979c8adcb978c154a064cdd4ad9b63: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.22">Neh 3:22</reference> <div eID="gen6524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6525" type="x-p"/> Farther northwards repaired the priests, the men of the district of Jordan. כּכּר does not, as Bertheau infers from <reference osisRef="Neh.12.28">Neh 12:28</reference>, signify the country round Jerusalem, but here, as there, the valley of the Jordan. See rem. on <reference osisRef="Neh.12.28">Neh 12:28</reference> and on Gen 13:10. Hence this verse informs us that priests were then dwelling in the valley of the Jordan, probably in the neighbourhood of Jericho. The length of wall built by these priests is not further particularized.
entries.4f635bcf7cd2e5f1eec68f5de518e6cd410784a1: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.23">Neh 3:23</reference> <div eID="gen6525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6526" type="x-p"/> Further on repaired Benjamin and Hashub over against their house, and Azariah the son of Maaseiah, by his house. Nothing further is known of these individuals.
entries.c37a3c7b689c3b4580518c9d188872f46822e084: <reference osisRef="Neh.3.24-Neh.3.25">Neh 3:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen6526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6527" type="x-p"/> Next repaired Binnui the son of Henadad, a second portion from the house of Azariah, to the angle and to the corner; and further on (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.25">Neh 3:25</reference>) Palal the son of Uzzai, from opposite the angle and the high tower which stands out from the king’s house by the court of the prison. We join העליון to המּגדּל, though it is also verbally admissible to combine it with המּלך בּית, “the tower which stands out from the king’s upper house,” because nothing is known of an upper and lower king’s house. It would be more natural to assume (with Bertheau) that there was an upper and a lower tower at the court of the prison, but this is not implied by העליון. The word means first, high, elevated, and its use does not assume the existence of a lower tower; while the circumstance that the same tower is in <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh 3:27</reference> called the great (הגּדול) tells in favour of the meaning high in the present case. The court of the prison was, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.32.2">Jer 32:2</reference>, in or near the king’s house; it is also mentioned <reference osisRef="Jer.32.8">Jer 32:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.12">Jer 32:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1">Jer 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.21">Jer 37:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jer 38:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.13">Jer 38:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.28">Jer 38:28</reference>, and Jer 39:14. But from none of these passages can it be inferred, as by Bertheau, that it was situate in the neighbourhood of the temple.
